en: Preface to the *Phonology and Meaning of the Jewel Instructions of the Chan Forest* Regarding the single volume of the *Jewel Instructions*: formerly, the two masters Miaoxi and Zhuanan,

concerned that the Dharma-Ending Age would become turbid and that the monastic communities (*cónglín*) would decline, selected the virtuous words and noble deeds of the ancients and compiled them into this collection, hoping thereby to turn back the tide.

The Buddha-Sun reorganized the collapsing discipline of the teachings, enabling those of ordinary capacity to aspire toward practice through his words, so that their virtue and deeds might be renewed.
Although the compilation was thus completed, it had not yet been disseminated; for the destiny of the Dharma has its own timing, manifesting only when conditions are met.
Subsequently, there was Master Jingshan of Eastern Wu, who traveled to Yunju and obtained these fragmentary manuscripts from Master Zu’an, rejoicing in them.

Whatever I encountered was absorbed completely into my heart. My only regret was that the texts were incomplete from beginning to end, making it difficult to establish a coherent system of doctrine and meaning.

Therefore, I have once again undertaken this compilation, extensively searching for the words of former masters. These accumulated works comprise over three hundred pieces; from these, the precious instructions have emerged.

Among them, there are those that support and promote the Dharma transformation, provide admonitions to the monastic community, reform the corrupt practices within the monasteries, and warn the students.
For one as dull and ignorant as I, this compilation—how could it possibly be considered insignificant?
Alas, among those of rash and shallow disposition, there are many who, seeing that its prose is plain and easy, place it high upon their bookshelves and neglect it.

Is this not to betray the painstaking efforts of the former sages and the words they left behind like those cast into a ditch? (Jian) From the year Wushen, I took my leave of Master Xuelang at Wangshan in Suzhou.
Master Ting studied in Chang’an, attending upon various masters. Whenever there was a lecture on the Dharma-treasury, he never missed it;
through diligent and repeated practice, the simple and honest style of the Chan practitioners of that region still persists.
This collection alone is concise in expression yet rich in meaning, and its subjects are so extensive that beginners, being unfamiliar with them, may encounter obstacles and hesitations. At times—

There exists a *Yinyi* (Explanations of Sounds and Meanings) that has been transmitted through successive copying but not yet published. It has gradually fallen into error and corruption, with discrepancies as grave as the confusion between the characters "fish" (*yu*) and "ox" (*lu*).

For this reason, it was impossible to refrain from publishing the *Yinyi*. Now, as many copies exist within the mountains, I have selected those that are concise and essential to establish this definitive edition.

Furthermore, I have cross-referenced and verified this work against both internal and external scriptures, working by lamplight long into the night for months on end until the collation was finally complete.
When my fellow practitioners beheld this excellent edition, they commissioned its carving into printing blocks for circulation, so that future seekers might easily consult it.
Not daring to boast of my own meager learning, I have merely recorded its origins and development here.
Recorded on the third day of the second month of the year Yihai of the Chongzhen era by the Bhikṣu Dajian of Liangxi,
as a phonetic glossary for the *Chanlin Baoxun* (Precious Instructions from the Zen Forest).
The post-disciple bhikṣu of Yunqi, Dajian, has proofread this.
This preface is like the courtyard of a gate. "Chan-lin" (Zen Grove) refers to "chan" (dhyāna), which means meditative concentration;
"lin" (grove) refers to a forest. This is intended to mean those who are practitioners dwelling in the mountains and forests. Lake... [text fragment]

Like the currents of the ocean, they gather at monasteries (*caityas*) from all directions; sharing the same hall and living together, they form companionships to study and cultivate the practice of tranquility.
For this reason, it is called a "Zen grove" (*chánlín*).
Regarding "Precious Instructions" (*Pao-hsün*): "Precious" (*pao*) means cherished; "Instructions" (*hsün*) means admonitions.

This refers to the fact that all the excellent words and virtuous deeds recorded in this book are sufficient to awaken those who have not yet attained realization and to instruct those whose cultivation is not yet complete.
Thus, later students hold them as precious as the most rare jewels; it is for this reason they are so named, hence called "Precious Instructions."
The repeated use of the character "zhe" (者) is a term used for emphasis and confirmation; it is intended to recount the origins of this book.
"In the past, Miaoxi" (昔妙喜): "xi" (昔) refers to ancient times. "Miaoxi" (妙喜) was Chan Master Dahui Pujue Zonggao of Mount Jing in Lin'an Prefecture (present-day Hangzhou).
He was the son of the Xi family of Ningguo in Jiangdong (modern-day Xuancheng) and was a successor of Foguo.
Chan Master Keqin was the fifteenth-generation descendant of Nanyue. At thirteen, he entered school, yet he took no pleasure in secular classics.
He went to Dongshan Huiyun Monastery to visit Chan Master Huizhi. At seventeen, he shaved his head and donned the black robes of a monk.
Later, he went west of Yunju to the old site of the ancient Yunmen Temple, where he cleared away weeds to build a hermitage. He remained there for twenty years, reclaiming the land.
From Huxiang, he traveled to Mount Yangshan, where he met Chan Master Zhuan-an Gui. Together they composed over one hundred verses on ancient cases (songgu).
This *Baokun* is a collection from that period; it is found in detail in the twentieth fascicle of the *Tongzai*.
Chan Master Zhuan-an Shigui of Longxiang in Wenzhou was the son of the Shi family in Chengdu Prefecture.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Fuyan Qingyuan and belonged to the fifteenth generation below Nanyue.
Regarding "Chumao (Clearing the Thatch) at Jiangxi Yunmen": "Chumao" means to cut down grass.

This refers to the time when the two masters cleared away the thatch and grass on the old site of Yunmen Temple to build a hermitage for their reclusion, at which time they jointly compiled this book.
During the Chunxi era, I traveled to Yunju and obtained [this text] from the old monk Zu’an. “I” (予) means “myself” (我);
not using “myself” but using “I” (予) is a humble expression used between host and guest. Chunxi was the reign title of Emperor Xiaozong of the Song dynasty.
“Traveled” (遊) means to journey through; it refers to how Master Jingshan traveled abroad until he reached Yunmenshan on Mount Yunju.
This is the site of its former location. The elder monk Zu’ān obtained these precious instructions; however, Zu’ān’s clan, lineage, and dharma heirs remain unknown.

It is regrettable that, due to the passage of time, the text has been damaged by insects and is incomplete from beginning to end. "Regrettable" (xī) expresses a sigh of lamentation over this difficulty. As for "its" (qí): it refers to [the aforementioned].
This is a metaphorical expression for something damaged by insects. "Worms" refers to paper-eating insects;
it means lamenting that the precious instructions one has obtained have been damaged by bookworms over many years, such that the beginning and end, the top and bottom, cannot be fully preserved.
Later, some [of his words] appeared in recorded sayings (*yulu*) and biographies (*zhuanji*). Over a period of ten years, there were barely more than fifty pieces of "residual speech" (*yuyu*).
To speak of the secret and manifest true functions is called "speech" (*yu*); to collect various matters together is called a "record" (*lu*);

to extensively record events of the past and present is called a "biography" (*zhuan*); and to broadly chronicle the worthy and the unworthy is called a "record" (*ji*). "Barely" (*jin*) means just now; it refers to the time since he first obtained this book.
These incomplete chapters were partially recovered from various recorded sayings and biographies.
After ten years of accumulation, they now comprise just over fifty remaining sections.
He further took over Huanglong in Longxing Prefecture. Master Huanglong Hui Nan was a native of the Zhang family of Xinzhou;
he was a dharma successor of Shichuang Chuyuan and the eleventh generation under Mount Heng.
Descending further, he reached Fozhao of Qingyuan Prefecture—namely, Yuyang Monastery in Mingzhou.

Fozhao Deguang, the Chan Master Zhu’an, was the son of the Peng family of Linjiang County. He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Dahui Zonggao and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Heng.
He received the tonsure at Huaguang Monastery on East Mountain in his native prefecture under Master Ji, and later served Emperor Xiaozong.
In the eleventh month of the third year of the Chunxi era, an imperial edict summoned him to enter Xuande Hall to discourse on Chan.
In the fifth year of the Chunxi era, he was bestowed the title "Fozhao" (Buddha-Shining), which spread throughout the realm and caused the school's teachings to flourish greatly.
Chan Master Jiangu Xingji of Guoqing Temple in Taizhou, surnamed Yang and a native of that prefecture, was a dharma successor of Chan Master Jingyuan of Huguo Temple.
He belonged to the sixteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
"Jieqi Lue Sanbai pian" (Abridged and Compiled Collection of Three Hundred Pieces). "Still" (reng) means to restore; "jie" (section/limit) means to regulate;

"qi" (thatch/gather) means to repair and supplement. This refers to restoring and taking up the recorded sayings left behind by the various elders from Huanglong down to Fozhao and Jiantang, regulating and repairing them, and adding the previous fifty-odd pieces to accumulate a total of three hundred.
Regarding the sequence of what was attained, there is a priority and posteriority; yet, these are not ranked according to antiquity or modernity.
This refers to the auxiliary phrasing used when recording that the scrolls of what was attained have a chronological order, rather than following the principle of placing the ancient first.
The present work is for the sake of posterity, serving merely as a sequence of explanations and clarifications. This preface is divided into three sections;
from this point upward constitutes the Introduction (Nidāna).

In general, it is intended to lead students to eliminate worldly power, profit, and the notions of self and other, so that they may pursue the Way, Virtue, Benevolence, and Righteousness. "In general" (gài) means... (Note: The final character "概" appears to be a fragment or an incomplete thought in the source text.)

"Intent" (yi) means "to intend. "Briefly" (lüe) means "to abridge. "To pare" (xiāo) and "to delete" (shān) mean to remove. "Power" (shì) refers to "majestic power" (wēishì). "Profit" (lì) refers to "material gain" (cáilì).

"Self and others" (rénwǒ) is a designation for "this and that" (bǐcǐ). "Toward" (qù) means "to head toward"; it also means to advance and extend one's steps. "The Way" (dào) is the principle of what is naturally so regarding things and affairs;
it is that which all people follow together. "Virtue" (dé) means "attainment" (dé); it is the attainment within the mind through practicing the Way. "Benevolence" (rén) means—
The virtue of the mind; the principle of love. Righteousness (*yi*) is the regulation of the mind and the appropriateness of affairs.

Indeed, the general purport of this book is to cause students to eliminate the mind for power and profit, as well as notions of self and other, so that they may incline toward the Way (*dao*), Virtue (*de*), and righteous principles.
The word "only" (*er yi*) is a term signifying completion without remainder. This refers to the Treasure.
As for the meaning of "instruction" (*xùn*):
its literary patterns and principles (*wénlǐ*) are leisurely and easygoing, devoid of any traces of loftiness, hyperbole, remoteness, or eccentricity;

this extends the textual expression of the precious instructions. "Text" (*wén*) refers to written characters, and "principle" (*lǐ*) refers to systematic order. "Leisurely" (*yōuyóu*) describes a state of natural ease.
"Peaceful and simple. "Haughty and extravagant" (*gāodàn*): "haughty" (*gāo*) means solitary, precarious, and towering; "extravagant" (*dàn*) also means deceptive and false.

"Wasteland" (*huāng*) means overgrown with weeds; "deceitful" (*guǐ*) means fraudulent. This refers to the fact that the characters and the structural logic of this book are leisurely and self-assured, peaceful and simple.
There is such goodness herein; there are no solitary, perilous, vain, extravagant, desolate, or unfounded words, nor any records of haughty, arrogant, deceitful, strange, or groundless deeds.
"It can truly assist in the far-reaching plan for entering the Way"—this speaks deeply of its efficacy.
"Can" (*kě*) indicates that while it is accessible, there are words suggesting it does not exhaust the subject. "Yóu" (猷) means method (*fǎ*) or the Way (*dào*).
This means that the text of this book is plain and simple, and it can truly serve as a methodological aid for students to enter the Way. The above constitutes the orthodox teaching.
This concludes the section; the following is the section on circulation.
I shall now carve it upon wood to propagate it widely. There will surely be those of like mind who, upon seeing it once, will grant their hearts’ assent.

"Though I may grow old and die in the hills and valleys, my aspirations will be fulfilled. Furthermore, "qián" (權) means temporary; it is a term used for that which is provisional and not necessarily so.
"Shì" (士) refers to one who possesses the reputation for practicing righteousness. "Xǔ" (許) means to grant or to comply with. "Qiū" (丘) refers to the high mounds of earth.
"Hè" (壑) refers to a place where there is water it is called a marsh (*zé*); where there is no water, it is called a valley (*hè*). "Zhì" (志) refers to the mind's—
"Zhī" (之所) refers to where one is headed. "Yuàn" (願) means that one’s sentiments are rare and cherished.
This implies that I intend to carve this book onto woodblocks and print it for wide circulation so that it does not remain stagnant.

Should there be scholars who share my same aspirations and, upon seeing this book, find their hearts in full accord with it, then even though I may grow old and die amidst hills and valleys, my heart's resolve and wishes will be fulfilled.
"Yi. "Dongwu" refers to the place where the śramaṇa Jingshan was located; "Suzhou" is the name of a commandery in Dongwu. "Śramaṇa" is a phonetic abbreviation of a Sanskrit term;
the full term is *śramaṇa*, which translates as "diligent in cessation. This means to diligently practice wholesome dharmas and to extinguish all [afflictions].
"Evil. "Pure Goodness" (Jingshan) is the posthumous name of the author; later students should not refer to him by both names simultaneously, but should instead say "Upper Jingshan, Lower Shan.
He was a native of Eastern Wu. As for the term *shū* (book/record): it means "to resemble" (*nyo*). It refers to recording events in accordance with the intent of the person [who experienced them].
Furthermore, it means "to unfold" (*shu*). Liu Xie said: "To unfold and arrange one's words and set them down upon tablets and slips is called *shū*."
● "Volume" (*juan*) refers to a fascicle (*juan*). It signifies that while the rolled-up state is many, the unrolled state is few. "Upper" (*shang*) carries the meaning of relative opposition;
where there is an upper, there must be a lower.
Chan Master Mingjiao Qisong of Furi Monastery in Hangzhou, whose courtesy name was Zhongling and self-styled name was Qianzi, was the son of the Li family from Tanzhen in Tengzhou.
He was a dharma successor of Xiaocong of Dongshan, the tenth generation in the lineage of Qingyuan.

He entered the monastic life at the age of seven, received full ordination at thirteen, and began his travels to seek teachers at nineteen. He constantly carried a scroll of the Avalokiteśvara Sūtra and recited it daily.

He recited the names of the Buddhas one hundred thousand times as his daily practice. He perused all the secular scriptures and treatises without exception and composed the *Yuanjiao lun* (Treatise on the Origin of the Teachings) in over one hundred thousand words.
In this work, he demonstrated that the Way of Confucianism and Buddhism are one and the same, thereby countering the arguments of Han Yu who sought to exclude Buddhism.
Wang Gong Su, Director of the Longtu Pavilion for the Kaifeng Prefecture, along with Ouyang Xiu and Cheng Shimeng, submitted [the work] for imperial review.

Emperor Renzong read it and expressed great admiration, ordering it to be included in the imperial canon by the editorial office. It was titled *Fujiao pian* (Three Volumes on Aiding the Teaching) and he was granted the purple robe, the square-cut cassock, and the title "Mingjiao" (Illuminator of the Teaching).
The Sanskrit original name for *heshang* is *upādhyāya*. Transmitted from Khotan, it was translated as *heshang*;

transmitted to this land [China], it was translated as "Power-Born" (*lìshēng*). This refers to those who have left the household life, meaning that by the power of their teacher, they are born and grow within the Dharma-body.
It produces the wealth of merit and nourishes the life-force of wisdom; therefore, it is called "powerfully born" (*ryōshō*).
It is revered, honored, and esteemed.

That the mind of the Way (*dōshin*) penetrates is called the "Way" (*dō*); furthermore, the perfection of its name is termed the "Way. This is precisely the subtle and wondrous Way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
In Confucianism, this refers to the subtle Way of "gracefully holding to the Mean.
Virtue (*de*) means rectifying the person; it is what is called establishing one's character. Monastics possess the precepts, meditative concentration, and wisdom;
Confucians possess filial piety, fraternal respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness—all of these are termed virtue.
"A single man" (*pifu*) is a designation for one who is destitute and solitary. Among the three armies, a commander may be taken away;
yet the will of a single man cannot be taken away. [Note: This is because the valor of the three armies resides in others, whereas the will of a single man resides in himself.

"King" (Wáng; the final syllable is pronounced with a departing tone). Generally, anyone who rules over the world is addressed as a "King. Furthermore, one who personally presides over the four seas is called a King.
Boyi and Shuqi were the two sons of the Lord of Guzhu. Guzhu was the territory enfeoffed by King Tang of Yin.
He was the ruler of the state. His clan name was Motaishì; his given name was Chū; his courtesy name was Ziqī. His eldest son, Bóyí, was named Yǔn and styled Gōngxìn.

His younger son, Shùqí, was named Zhì and styled Gōngdá. They were posthumously titled Bóyí and Shùqí. When their father was about to pass away, he left a testament to establish Shùqí as his successor.
Shùqí, regarding the natural order of kinship as paramount, said: "If I were to occupy the throne, it would be contrary to righteousness."
Bo Yi held his father’s command to be supreme; I, however, am unfilial while remaining in office. Both men fled. The people of the state installed Bo Yi’s middle son as their ruler.
When the two brothers heard that Chang, the Chief of the West, was skilled at caring for the elderly, they said, "Why do we not go and join him?
After King Wen passed away, King Wu launched an expedition against Zhou. The two brothers struck the horse's head and remonstrated, saying, "While your father is still not yet buried—"
They buried him, even using shields and spears; can this be called filial piety? To assassinate a sovereign with a minister’s title—can this be called loyalty?
His attendants wished to execute him, but the Grand Duke said, "This is a man of righteousness," and he helped him away.

After King Wu pacified the world and the Zhou became the hegemon, Bo Yi and Shu Qi were ashamed to eat the grain of Zhou; they subsequently retired to Mount Shouyang, where they gathered *wei* sprouts to eat.
In the end, they starved to death. Shi Yong said: "The two brothers of Guzhu were ashamed of war; seeing the dust of the advancing army, they blocked the road and begged for a ceasefire.
When Mount Shouyang collapsed and became level ground, it was surely because no one spoke their names."

Jie of Xia, named Lügui, was the son of Emperor Fa. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who harms many people and kills excessively is called "Jie. He was dissolute, licentious, and devoid of the Way.
He obtained the daughter of the Shi clan, named Meixi, and constructed towers of jasper and terraces of jade to indulge his pleasures to the utmost.

He created a wine-pool upon which boats could be rowed, and the mound of dregs could be seen for ten li. Longfeng remonstrated with him out of loyalty, but Jie did not follow his advice and killed him. [This was the end of] Yin.
Tang possessed virtue. Yi Yin assisted Tang in attacking Jie. Jie was defeated in battle and fled to the state of Sanzong.
Tang pursued and attacked him again, banishing Jie to Nanchao where he died. From Yu to Jie, there were seventeen generations.
The dynasty lasted for four hundred and thirty-two years.

The Shang ruler Zhou was named Xin, also known as Shou. He was the son of Emperor Yi. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), the title Zhou is given to one who is cruel in righteousness and destructive to goodness.
He obtained the daughter of the Su clan, Daji, and cherished her exceedingly. He established a wine-pool and a forest of meat, causing men and women to pursue one another therein in the nude.
He constructed the Palace of Long Nights, where one hundred and ten days constituted a single day. He employed the "roasting and branding" punishment;

he剖開 (pòu kāi) pregnant women and castrated those who had reached sexual maturity. He built the Lu Terrace, which took seven years to complete. His deeds brought harm to the loyal and virtuous. [End of] Subject.
Shu Bi Gan exhausted his loyalty in offering remonstrance, and consequently had his heart cut out and died. Grand Preceptor Ji Zi feigned madness and became a slave.
His elder brother, Wei Zi, considering the loss of benevolence, fled from him. Later, King Wu raised an army to attack him;
having defeated him, he ascended the Lu Tai terrace, covered his head, threw himself into the fire, and died. From Tang to Zhou, there were thirty [generations] in total.
The world [endured] for six hundred and twenty-nine years. Shi Yong said: "Grain accumulated until it became dust, yet in the end it was not opened;

who would have known that rejecting counsel would destroy such brilliant talent? When King Wu’s army rose, there was no one to oppose him; thus he became but a heap of ashes on the outskirts of Shang."

King You of Zhou named his palace Nie. He was the son of King Xuan. According to the *Shi Fa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who obstructs and blocks so that communication is impossible is called "You.
It is likely because his administration was tyrannical toward the people that Mount Qi collapsed of its own accord, and the waters of the mountains and rivers dried up.
He obtained a woman from the state of Bao named Baoji and took her as his favorite. Consequently, he degraded Queen Shen and the Crown Prince Yijiu. Baoji did not like to laugh; at Li...
Mount Shang raised a fire to mockingly provoke the smile of Bao Si. Later, Shen Hou grew enraged and summoned the Qunrong tribes to slaughter [the Zhou] at the foot of Mount Li.
Shi Yong said: "Relying on her favor, she acted with much artifice and enjoyed total freedom; she raised a fire on Mount Li as a game for the feudal lords.
How could she have known that a single laugh would topple the state? Unaware, the dust of the barbarians filled the Jade Towers."
King Zhou Li’s name was Hu; he was the son of King Yi. According to the *Shifa* (Canon of Posthumous Titles), one who slaughters the innocent is titled “Li.

The king acted without the Way, being extravagant, arrogant, and tyrannical. The people of the state slandered him, so the king appointed the Minister of Guard (Wei Wu) to oversee the slanders, ordering that anyone who slandered him be executed.
Duke Shao remonstrated with him, saying: "By silencing the mouths below, you are causing your transgressions above to increase. I fear this will bring ruin upon the altars of the land and grain."
Yu was grieved. The King would not listen, and the people of the state rebelled against him. Calamity befell the King, who then fled to Zhi. The Crown Prince was young;
the two dukes, Zhou and Shao, remained in harmonious accord as they jointly managed the affairs of state, which is why this period is called the "Joint Regency" (Gonghe).
The twenty-two pieces of the *Xiaoya* all concerned the virtuous governance of Wen, Wu, Cheng, and Kang; by this time, they had all fallen into total disuse.
Xin Yu said to Emperor Taizong of Tang: "Jie and Zhou were the Son of Heaven;
yet if their names were applied to a commoner, that person would be angry. Yan Hui and Min Ziqian were commoners;
yet if their names were applied to the Son of Heaven, he would be pleased. What is valued is virtue, not rank."
"Affliction" (*huàn*) refers to sorrow.

○ "Sage" (*shèng*) means one whose spiritual intelligence is clear and penetrating; it is called "sage" because they instruct others with correctness. Furthermore, "sage" implies correctness. They teach people through what is correct.
"Worthy" (*xián*) surpasses the ordinary and approaches the sage; thus, one is called "worthy."
"Learning is learning. It is the desire to know what is already known and to know what is not yet known, and to be able to do what has not yet been mastered.

Through learning one gathers [knowledge]; the gentleman learns to gather it. He uses inquiry to discern it, dwells in it with broad-mindedness, and practices it with benevolence. The commentary states:
"When a sage is in a position below [the throne], though his virtue is manifest, he has not yet attained his proper station; thus he advances in virtue and cultivates himself."
This is simply a matter of karma. To accumulate learning and engage in inquiry and debate is to advance one's practice. To dwell in spaciousness and practice benevolence is to cultivate virtue.

Furthermore, regarding the accumulation of learning and inquiry through debate: if a person does not apply themselves to study, they will have no means to synthesize the various principles and will merely possess them within themselves as isolated fragments.
If one studies without inquiring, there is no way to distinguish between the various principles so that their respective categories remain orderly and unconfused.

Regarding the refined and the coarse, the fundamental and the derivative, one may not know how to choose between them. This is derived from the text of the second line of the *Jiuzhi* hexagram in the *Yijing*.
"To supplement" means to assist.
As for "daily renewal," the inscription on King Tang’s basin says: "If one renews oneself today, let there be daily renewal; and again, daily renewal. However, this refers to that [other context].
The scholar advances in their studies and cultivates virtue, thereby transforming themselves anew. It is like bathing one's body to wash away the filth of past stains and renewing oneself.
This passage is from the *Daxue*.
The Grand Historian (Taishigong) was surnamed Sima and named Tan; he served as the Grand Historian (Taishiling). His son, named Qian, succeeded him in his father’s office.
Because he honored his father, he was styled "Gong" (the Venerable). He was a native of Longmen in the Western Han.
Mencius, whose name was Ke and courtesy name Ziyu, was a native of the state of Zou. He composed the *Book of Mencius* in seven chapters, comprising two volumes, the upper and the lower.
King Hui of Liang was Marquis Wen of Wei; his capital was Daliang, where he usurped the title of King. His posthumous title was Hui. (From the *Records of the Grand Historian*)
In the thirty-fifth year of King Hui’s reign, he humbled his etiquette and increased his gifts to attract men of virtue, and Mencius arrived.
King Liang asked him, saying, "Elder sir, you have come from no less than a thousand li away; how can you benefit my state? Mencius replied:
"Why must the King speak only of profit? There is simply benevolence (ren) and righteousness (yi).
When the King asks about the intent behind strengthening the army and enriching the state, Mencius’s response is that he does not regard wealth as profit; rather, he regards righteousness as profit."
"Rarely speaking of profit" means that such instances are few. He rarely spoke of profit, destiny, and benevolence. The principle of destiny is subtle; the way of benevolence is vast;

and profit is harmful to righteousness. It is said that the Sage feared students would become mired in profit, using it to extinguish the public good, becoming greedy for gain at the expense of righteousness, and sinking into base depravity; therefore, he spoke of them rarely.
The honored and the honored—these are the Son of Heaven. The poor and the lowly—these are the common people.
From the Son of Heaven down to the common people, all are equally afflicted by the malady of greed for profit; what difference is there between them?
This is a flaw. Now, words that "receive from above and initiate below" are contrary to principle and subvert the laws of propriety;
is this not indeed so? It is a manifestation of [unrestrained] expansion.
"Subjugate" means to take by force.
○ The Discourse on the Lower Section of "Having Form" states: "Evil with form has a definite source from which it comes; its adversary can be resisted.
Evil without form comes from an unpredictable source; its harm is not slight. Therefore, the evil of killing people is small [compared to this]."
The evil of harming others is great. One who kills a person is described in terms of outward traces; one who harms another is described in terms of the heart.
Though the trace may be that of killing, the transgression can be excused; yet when one harbors a cruel heart that harms the Way, the calamity is most extreme.
For this reason, manifest evil has form and is clearly visible, while formless evil is obscure and unfathomable. Because of this, [the nature of] human beings...
Because it can be seen and known, it is considered light and small; because no one sees it and no one knows it, it is considered heavy and great.
"Youyan" (遊晏) means leisurely enjoyment; it is a banquet where host and guest rejoice together in tranquility.
The *hen* is the name of a poisonous bird. Its shape is like that of a chicken; its color is purple-green. Its neck is eight inches long, and it feeds on snakes and vipers.
When its feathers and plumage pass through food and drink, whoever consumes such food will die.
The *ge* and the *mao* are both weapons of war. The *ge* is a leveled-headed halberd, six feet six inches long. The *mao* is two zhang long;
its shape is like a hook. Both are instruments for inflicting injury upon others.
The main chamber at the rear of the hall is called the *táng*; the deep innermost part is called the *ào*.

The Great Sage Confucius did not attain the throne, yet he left behind the record of his execution of Zheng Mao; although the Duke of Zhou was a sage, he left behind the record of his execution of Guan and Cai;

He answered him. The Master attained realization upon these words and presented a verse, saying: "One who studies the Way must be an iron man;
when the hand touches the heart, judgment is immediate. Directly seize unexcelled Bodhi; do not concern yourself with any right or wrong.
Thereafter, he became a spiritual friend to Ciming.
Guanghui Lian, Chan Master Yuanlian of Guanghui Monastery in Ruizhou, was the son of the Chen family of Quanzhou.
He was a successor of Chan Master Shoushan Nian and belongs to the ninth generation under Mount Heng.
"Ji" (激) means to stimulate; "yang" (揚) means to raise up. This conveys the principle of "stimulating the turbid and raising the pure.
It means that those who are muddled and turbid are stimulated so that they may exert themselves, while those who are clean and pure are raised up so that they may be easily seen.
Banban Ming (Bānbān Míng). Section.
Regarding Doushuai Yue of Longxing Prefecture: Chan Master Doushuai Congyue was the son of the Xiong family of Ganzhou;
he was a successor of Chan Master Zhenjing Wen and belongs to the thirteenth generation under Nanyue.
"Knocking at the gate and striking the joints": "knocking at the gate" refers to the critical juncture where one passes through that which is difficult to pass;

"striking the joints" refers to the points of obstruction where one penetrates that which is otherwise impassable. This means to strike its pivotal mechanism and hit its essential joints, thereby upholding the ancestral seal.
He reveals the true mechanism and strikes at the essential points to bring about joy and liberation.
How could this be done in vain?
Zhang Wugou, Minister Zhang Jiucheng, styled Zishao and titled the Layman Wugou, was from Hangzhou’s Salt... [text truncated]
The Official: He received the Dharma from Chan Master Miaoxi Gaofeng.
Li Hanlao, the Vice Director of the Council of State; Li Bing’s courtesy name was Hanlao. He received the Dharma from Chan Master Miaoxi.
Lu Juren’s surname was Lü; his given name was Benchong, and his courtesy name was Juren. He sought the Way from Chan Master Miaoxi Gao.
His official rank reached that of Hanlin Academician.
Those among his disciples who had entered his inner chambers would request further instruction and inquire about the Way, seeking to resolve their doubts regarding the profound mysteries of Chan.
A "friend beyond the mundane" (*fangwai you*) is one who has emerged from the dust and toil of the world, having escaped from the constraints of ordinary sentiments;
thus, they are called a friend beyond the mundane.
Like the striking of thunder and the sweeping of lightning: when thunder strikes, it disperses [clouds] across the vast sky; when lightning sweeps, it eradicates all malevolent spirits. Indeed...
Affectionate love, whether favorable or adverse, is utterly pure.
*Rèn* refers to the lapel of a garment. *Pìyì* describes an appearance of being startled, terrified, and losing one's composure.
*Yáysǐ* refers to the boundaries of water; it signifies that [the matter] cannot be fathomed or measured.
"Ni" (擬) means to estimate or conjecture.
"Shū" (書) is pronounced "cì" (刺) in the fourth tone; since ancient times, paper did not exist, so people carved names and surnames into bamboo or wood.
"Tián" (恬) means tranquil and peaceful. "Něi" (餒) is pronounced with the "nú" (奴) and "zuì" (罪) finals; it means hunger.
"Bending the waist" refers to the posture of bowing. During the Jin dynasty, there was Tao Qian, styled Yuanming and nicknamed Yuanliang.
He grew five willow trees at his gate and called himself Master Willow-Branches. Serving as Magistrate of Pengze, he was simple and noble by nature and would not privately attend to his superiors.
One day, a district supervisor (*duyou*) arrived at the county seat. An official told him that he ought to gird his belt and see him. Yuanming sighed and said:
"How could I, for the sake of five pecks of rice, bend my waist before the petty children of my village?

This very day I shall untie my sash and resign from office, composing the 'Return and Depart' (Guiqulai Ci) poem. The historian Yong wrote: "An eminent talent—how could he endure being humbled by a low-ranking official?
Five willows planted at his gate, his affairs are now desolate. A phoenix does not compete with a chicken for food; do not blame the Master for being too lazy to bow his waist."

This refers to the manner of one who carries a broom and sweeps the ground. When the Han Gaozu ascended the throne, he visited his father, the Grand Duke (Taigong), once every five days, treating him according to the rites between father and son.
His household steward said to the Grand Duke: "Although Gaozu is your son, he is now the sovereign."
Although Grandfather Tai was his father, he was still a subject. How could a sovereign bow to a subject? If this were done, the gravity of his majesty would not be maintained.
Later, when Emperor Gaozu visited Grandfather Tai’s court, Tai swept the path with a broom and met him at the gate, stepping backward as he approached.
Gaozu was greatly startled and descended from his carriage to support him. Grandfather Tai said, "Emperor! You are the sovereign. Why do you bring disorder to the Way of Heaven by acting thus?"
Following this principle, the High Ancestor then honored the Duke of Tai as the August Emperor (Taishang Huangdi).
He approved the words of the Master of the Household and bestowed upon him five hundred catties of gold.
"Suan-han" (酸寒) describes the state of being terrified; it refers to the body shivering and the heart chilling.
"Ju-ji" (跼蹐): the former means to bend the body; the latter means to plant one's feet closely together while taking small steps.
This refers to a person in fear whose body dares not extend itself and whose feet dare not relax their stance; such is the nature of flattery and servility.
"Zhōng" (鍾) means to gather together. "Shēn" (申) means to clarify or manifest. "Chéng" (呈) means to present.
"Móbài" (膜拜) refers to prostrating and kneeling for a long time. "Zhū" (誅) means to execute someone by clarifying their crimes and putting them to death;
thus it is called "zhū. "Lù" (錄) means to record and collect their names while investigating their offenses; thus it is called "lù."
To redeem one's offense by paying a fine is called "ransom" (shu).

On the eighth month of the Gengchen year, the first year of the Jianyuan era of Emperor Gaozu of the Qi dynasty, the monk Sengyuan arrived at Mount Zhong as the Emperor went there on an official visit.
By chance, the Emperor visited the śramaṇa Sengyuan. Sengyuan sat upon his couch and declined to receive him, citing old age and illness.
The High Ancestor intended to go beneath the couch to see him, but his attendants said, "The room and bed are narrow and cramped; they cannot accommodate a palanquin or a ceremonial canopy.
Thereupon, he halted the carriage and departed after making his inquiries with great earnestness. Furthermore, Sengyuan had resided in the mountains for over fifty years; at first, he drank...
His food did not suffice for his needs; he drank from mountain streams and ate wild fruits for more than twenty years. People from all quarters looked up to his lofty character.
On the day of his death, a memorial was presented to the Emperor, who subsequently appointed him as a state preceptor and provided a state funeral at Mount Zhongshan.
Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu, Donglin, and Huxi. He was the son of the Jia family of Loufan in Yanmen.
In the fifth year of the Taiyuan era of Emperor Xiaowu of the Jin dynasty, due to the chaos caused by the Qin, he had not yet returned to the Jin territory.

In his youth, he was a Confucian scholar who was extensively versed in the Six Classics and particularly profound in the *Book of Changes* (*Zhouyi*). Once, while visiting his younger brother Huichi, he went to the seat of Dharma Master Dao’an.
Later, upon hearing a discourse on the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he exclaimed with joy and admiration: "The Nine Schools of Confucianism and Daoism are but mere chaff.

He subsequently shaved his head to leave the household life and took it as his personal mission to propagate the Great Dharma. Hui’an had over a thousand disciples, and the Master occupied the foremost seat among them.
When the region of Guanzhong was thrown into turmoil, Dao’an dispersed his disciples. The Master traveled south to Xunyang, where he saw Mount Kuang and took a liking to it;
he built a thatched hut among the mountains. The local governor, Minister Huan Yin, revered his virtue and character and established a vihāra for him. One night—
Thunder and wind uprooted trees and stirred the sands, leveling the foundations of the earth and casting timber upon it as if by divine operation.
His reputation for the Way grew ever more exalted. During the decline of the Jin dynasty, men of extraordinary talent throughout the realm lived in seclusion and refused office.

The Master established the Lotus Society, gathering various worthy scholars and over a thousand *śramaṇas* to seek rebirth in the Pure Land. This was during the reign of Emperor An of the Eastern Jin.
When the Emperor visited Xunyang, he issued an imperial decree for Huiyuan to come forth once. The Master declined on the grounds of old age and illness and did not go out.

The Emperor’s respect increased all the more, and he commanded the Governor of Jiujiang to provide the necessities for his practice at the appropriate times of the year. He lived there for thirty years, never venturing beyond the mountain.
Whenever he received guests, the Tiger Brook Bridge served as the limit. A few days before his death, celestial music came to welcome him.
He sat facing west and passed away at the age of eighty-three. He authored the *Kuāngshān jí* (Collected Works of Kuāngshān) in thirty fascicles, which remains widely circulated in the world.
○ Yuánjí Cén: Chan Master Yuánjí Yàncén of Tàipíng Prefecture, from Tái City in Fǔ Prefecture.
Ren succeeded Chan Master Faru of Yunju; he was the sixteenth generation descendant of Nanyue.
A preface is called a "xu" (序), and a postscript is called a "ba" (跋).
As for the term "dianxing" (典刑), Mencius said: "Taijia overthrew the *dianxing* of Tang," meaning that a sage rectifies the violent.
"Eliminating disorder" means to punish evil and remove what is improper; it is the method and standard for encouraging goodness.
"Ji" (幾) means "near" or "about to. "Sweeping the ground" refers to the collapse and ruin of the teachings.
Wang Manzi was merely speaking in the vernacular; he is but a servant within this Dharma-gate.
"Zhengui" (箴規) signifies sincerity; it is also rendered as "medicinal needles," for they are able to eliminate poisonous ailments.
"Zui" means stupor and delusion.
○ Dongshan Kong (Dongshan Huikong Chanshi) of Xuefeng, Fuzhou: a native of the Chen clan of that prefecture, he was a successor of Chan Master Letan Shanqing.
He belonged to the fourteenth generation under Nanyue. In his youth, he shaved his head and donned the black robes of a monk.
Shaking his mendicant’s staff (*khakkhara*), he traveled to various regions; he attained realization at Caotang and propagated the Dharma at Xuefeng.
This refers to providing assistance.
As for "forgetting," it is from the "Great Master" chapter of *Zhuangzi*: Confucius said, "Fish forget each other in rivers and lakes; birds [forget each other in the sky]."

They forget one another in the void; people forget one another in the Way and its arts. The commentary states: When the water is deep and they swim therein, the fish find their joy and thus forget one another.
When the Way is vast and boundless, both self and others are extinguished; people find their joy and thus forget one another.
"Fén" (閩) is the name for the region of Fújiàn.
"Shāngfù" (償負) means to repay; to borrow money and fail to repay it is called "fù" (負).
○ Zhèwēng Yǎn (浙翁琰), the Chan Master Ruyǎn of Zhōngshān in Jīnlíng, was styled Zhèwēng. His dharma lineage is not clearly known.
To pardon those with crimes and release them entirely is called "shè" (pardon). [The details of] Càn’s seclusion in the mountains are unknown.
The ancient Master Bǎo of Dòngshān in Ruìzhōu was a native of Lúzhōu; he succeeded the Zen Master Jiè of the Fifth Patriarch.
The ninth generation descendant of Qingyuan was a man of strict integrity. He once served as the head of the storehouse (kūsī) under the Fifth Patriarch.

On one occasion, the Precept Master (Jiè) fell ill and ordered an attendant to go into the storehouse to fetch fresh ginger for his medicine. Baoshou rebuked him. The attendant reported this to the Precept Master, who ordered that money be taken back to purchase it.
Only then did Baoshou take the ginger and give it to him. Later, the position of abbot at Dongshan in Junzhou became vacant; the local magistrate...
Baoshou entrusted the precepts to Shu, and Zhizhe, whom he had recommended, was appointed as the abbot. The precepts stated: "The man who sells ginger shall reside at De.

Subsequently, he left the world and resided at Dongshan; later, he moved to Guizong Temple. One day, as he was leaving the gate, he saw an official riding a horse approaching. The Master asked, "What official is this?
The attendant replied, "It is the County Magistrate (Xianwei); he orders us to clear the road. Baoshou stood to one side on the left of the path to avoid him.
When he reached it, the horse suddenly saw him, knelt down, and would not go forward. Huibao said, "Even a beast recognizes a man.
The magistrate realized this was Huibao; he bowed twice and departed. Later, when Huibao moved to Yunju, one night a mountain deity carried his sedan chair and walked around the temple. Huibao said:

"Carry your father and mother. "Carry them up to the abbot's quarters. When Huibao was first traveling as a wandering monk (*cankṣu*), he once stayed overnight at an inn and was harassed by a courtesan.
He then yielded his bed to her to sleep upon. That night, Huibao sat upright in meditation until dawn. When the courtesan demanded payment for the lodging, Huibao gave it to her.
As she was leaving the door, she took fire and set his mat ablaze before departing. The courtesan reported the matter as it truly was.
He informed his mother and subsequently invited a master to perform a vegetarian feast and seek repentance on his behalf; thus he was called a true son of the Buddha.

He once composed a eulogy for Bodhidharma that became most widely circulated within the monastic communities. Master Langye Huijue recognized its excellence, and it is now included in the *Zhengfayan zang* (Treasury of the True Dharma Eye).
*Ju* (踞) means to sit upon a great seat. *Fan* (泛) means abundant; it also means floating.

*Chà* (刹) is a Sanskrit term for *khaṭvāṅga*; here it refers to a staff, specifically the pole for a banner. According to the *Chuyao lan* (出要覽), whenever a śramaṇa attains the Way, he erects a banner to announce his achievement to the four quarters.

Xuetang went to Wugu Mountain in Quzhou. Chan Master Xuetang Daoheng was the son of the Ye family of Xunzhou.
He succeeded Chan Master Foyuan of Fuyan, the fifteenth generation under Nanyue, following the current of the lineage; this is now referred to as the "Single Path.
Basan Ben, whose secular name was from Jianfu Monastery in Raozhou, was a native of Jiangzhou. He previously resided at Boshan and succeeded [the aforementioned master].
Master Dahui was the sixteenth generation descendant of Nanyue.

Upon entering the temple, one finds that the six paths leading down are wide and spacious; the quarters are pleasant, the corridors and galleries are well-maintained, and the overall construction is excellent.
The incense and lamps are unceasing; this is good for repaying kindness. The bells and drums are distinct; this is good for the monastic regulations. The gruel and rice are pure and clean;
this is good for the assembly of those who receive grace. The monks’ conduct is courteous; this is good for the rules of decorum.
Regarding Zhang Xiyan’s service during the Song dynasty: Zhang Xiyan served as the Magistrate of Pingxiang County.

Fan Yanling was a Palace Attendant (Dianzhi) escorting troops through Jinling. Zhang Yong, having been appointed by imperial decree to oversee the affairs of Jinling, asked him, "Have you seen any good officials along your route?
He replied, "Yesterday I passed through Pingxiang; its Magistrate, Zhang Xiyan, is a fine official."

Yong said, "How can one know that it is good? He replied, "Since entering this territory, the bridges and roads have been perfect, the fields and gardens are wide and open, there are no farmers neglecting their work in the wilds, and there is no gambling in the markets.
Hearing the clear sounding of the night watches and drums, one surely knows there is excellent governance.
Yong said, "To emulate Yan Hui is certainly virtuous, but Your Excellency is also a fine official. Thus it was.
On the same day, they were both presented at court: Xiyan was appointed as the Commissioner for Transport, and Yanling as a Court Gate Marquis.
This was the result achieved by Zhang Yong, whose courtesy name was Fuzhi and who was later posthumously enfeoffed as the Duke of Dingguo.
"Your Excellency" (Kaksha) is a term of address. Furthermore, the *Yulu* states: "The Chancellor, the Three Ducal Ministers, and the Prefectural Governor are all addressed as 'Your Excellency'.
Regarding the character for "bank" (*ge*), the upper part signifies the meaning of firmness and solidity, while the lower part refers to the embankment of a pond.
"Ruìsàn" (潰散) means to scatter and disperse;
it does not merely mean to be out of alignment. ○ "Wēijìn" (煨燼): the lower character is pronounced *jǐn*.
It refers to the remains of a fire. ○ Huì'ān Guāng of Guīfēng in Xīnzhōu: Master Huì'ān Guāng was a native of Jiānníng. He succeeded Xuě... [Snow Mountain].
As for Chan Master Tangxing Ji:
"Weak-crested" (ruòguàn) refers to those under twenty; since the ancient custom was to wear the cap at age twenty, this term refers to those aged fifteen or sixteen who have not yet been capped.
He wore the great sash (*dàdài*). Furthermore, every sash must have its pendant ornaments (*pèi*). Whenever the ancients encountered virtuous deeds or excellent words, they would immediately—
They are inscribed on the pendants to show that one must not forget them;

they serve as a standard for the laws. Furthermore, "standard" (zhun) refers to that by which one measures levelness and governs correctness. The commentary states: "One sets up water to observe the line;
taking water as the standard of levelness constitutes the instrument for leveling."
“Màn” means empty; it means to deceive. It means to stand firm, transcendent, and independent.
Furthermore, Chan Master Qiān-ān Shǒurén was a native of Shangyú in Yuè.
He was the dharma heir of Chan Master Xuétáng Xíng and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Nányuè.
"Pho" (頗) refers to an improper appearance. "Jiu" (就) means to follow or indulge.
"Qi" (啟) and "di" (迪) mean to enlighten and guide.
○ Ying’ān Huá: Chan Master Ying’ān Tánhuá of Tiantong in Mingzhou. He was the son of the Wáng family of Qí Prefecture.
He succeeded Chan Master Long of Huqiu; he was the sixteenth generation descendant of Nanyue.
*Zhi* (志) refers to the superior mind above, while *qi* (氣) refers to the vital energy below. By nourishing the mind through principle, the will does not grow clouded;
by leading the energy with the will, the energy does not fall into disorder. As the discourse says: "One whose energy obeys the commands of the mind is a worthy person. When the mind obeys..."
Those who entrust their lives to their vital energy (qi) are petty people. Now, vital energy is the servant of the will; the will is the commander of vital energy.
If the mind follows the fluctuations of vital energy, then vital energy conversely becomes the commander of the will.
When vital energy acts as the commander, the will of my mind declines; this is for the mind to be enslaved by vital energy. Sages and noble gentlemen govern with the mind.
The vital energy (*qi*). One does not allow oneself to be governed by the *qi*, but uses the mind to direct the *qi*, rather than being moved by the *qi*.
*Puyun Yuan* (Self-Round of Puyun), Chan Master of Nankang Commandery, was the son of the Yong family of Mianzhou.
He succeeded Chan Master Nan’an Wu and belonged to the sixteenth generation under Mount Heng.

The Head Seat (shouzuo) serves as a model for the monastic community; he is the eye for humanity and the heavens, and by sharing the seat to preach the Dharma, he opens the way for future generations.
Hence, he is called the Head Seat.
As for the "one-talent monk" (yicai seng), his identity is not clearly known; some identify him as Shui'an.
The Secretary was in charge of literary correspondence. All matters concerning the monastery’s public notices, petitions, letters, and prayers at shrines were under his jurisdiction.
Fayun (Fashun) of Baiyang in Fuzhou: a native of the Wen family from Mianzhou; he was a successor of Fuyan.
Master Yuan was the fifteenth generation descendant of Nanyue. One day, the Master ascended the hall and said: "Good things arrive in layers upon layers;
there is no need for fabrication or contrivance. Yellow leaves falling in the forest are swept away by the water; white clouds drifting across the valley are rolled back by the wind.
With a single cry from the cold geese, worldly thoughts are severed; as soon as the frost-bell strikes, my mountain [is revealed]."
Cui said, "Baiyang has qualities that surpass others: throughout the night he tends the cold hearth, stirring the dead embers.
As the keeper of the Tripitaka, he is well-versed in both the scriptures and their underlying principles;
he constantly attends to the cases and catalogs, restoring what is missing and mending what is torn."
Fatong Wutou, Dharma Master Fatong of Beishan in Zhenzhou, was a successor of Chan Master Liaoching of Changlu.

As the Guest Prefect (Zhike), he was responsible for receiving guests; whenever monastics or laypeople encountered one another, he would attend to them with incense and tea, ensuring that all matters of reception and invitation were conducted with perfect order.
Chan Master Zhengxian Zhenmu of Nanguang County’s Guizong Monastery was a native of the Chen clan from Tongzhou.
He was a dharma successor of Chan Master Foyuan Yuan and belonged to the fifteenth generation of the Nanyue lineage.
The *vinaya-dhara* (Vina) serves as the leader who thoroughly manages the monastic community. Whether internal or external matters of the Sangha, there is none that he does not oversee.
"Vinaya-dhara" is a term that combines both the Indic and the Chinese; it refers to what is currently known as the *yuèzhòng* (Choir Master).
The Assistant Administrator was in charge of the monastery’s permanent assets, including gold, grain, money, and silk, as well as the accounting of incoming and outgoing rice and wheat,

maintaining a calendar for these matters accordingly. He was Chan Master De-yong of Shuanglin in Wuzhou, whose secular surname was Dai of that same prefecture, and who was a dharma heir of Chan Master Gao’an Shan-wu.
The term for *jian-si* (monastic supervisor) in Sanskrit is *karmadāna*, which here means "abbot" (*si-zhu*). This refers to the present-day *jian-si*.

In this office, one diligently attends to the incense and lamps morning and evening and receives officials. Having served with integrity, ability, and public conscientiousness, there are no grievances from those above or below.
It is filled to capacity.

Like the sea that receives all and the mountain that contains all, its capacity is like that of the great ocean; there is no water it does not receive. The mind is like a mountain valley; there is nothing it will not accommodate.
"Zan" (贊) means to assist and aid. "She" (社) refers to a sacrificial altar; "xi" (席) refers to a gathering or assembly.
"Xiao" (嘯) is the sound of blowing air; "lie" (冽) refers to a biting cold.
"Xiang" (驤) and "teng" (騰) describe the manner of leaping upward and soaring far away.
"The tiger roars and the dragon soars" refers to the fifth line of the *Qian* hexagram in the *Yi*: "The flying dragon is in the heavens; it is advantageous to see the great man.
What does this mean? The Master said: "Those of the same sound respond to one another; those of the same breath seek one another out. Water flows toward moisture; fire moves toward dryness.
Clouds follow the dragon; wind follows the tiger. When the sage arises, all things behold him. That which is rooted in Heaven is close to what is above."
That which belongs to the earth is intimate with what is below; thus each follows its own kind. Furthermore, a poem says:
"When those above and those below share the same virtue, wind and clouds meet in harmony. Like Heaven bestowing rain and dew, all things come to life in radiant splendor."
Yaoshan Weiyen, the Zen Master of Yao Mountain in Dingshui Prefecture, was the son of the Han family from Jangzhou and succeeded Zen Master Shitou Xiqian.
Tianhuang Daowu,
the Zen Master of Tianhuang in Jingzhou, was the son of the Zhang family from Dongyang in Wuzhou and succeeded [Zen Master Shitou].
The head monk:
"Yi" (翼) refers to the appearance of birds taking flight; "hong" (鴻) refers to the wild goose.
"Pai" (沛) refers to the appearance of water flowing down with great force. "Shan" (潸), pronounced like "shan," refers to the appearance of tears falling.
"Upholding the straight while practicing the Way, if one serves others by following the straight path, where could one go without being dismissed three times?
If one serves others by following a crooked path, why must one leave the state of one's parents? These are the words of Liu Xiaohui from the *Analects*.
"Chu-su" refers to rice made from grass seeds.
"Juan-juan" means anxious distress.
Regarding "xun-jie": ten days constitute a "xun," and twelve days constitute a "jie."
"Où" (Cou) refers to that which takes on the form of a human being.
Wàn’ān Jiāngzhōu Dōnglín Wàn’ān Dàoyán Chánshī was the son of the Xiè family of Tóngzhōu.
He was a successor of Chán Master Dàhuì Zǒnggǎo and belongs to the sixteenth generation under Nányuè.
Guanshouzu’s origins are unknown.
The "fu" (tally) follows the Han system, using bamboo six cun long that is split and then rejoined to serve as a token of trust.
A "lang" is so called because it is greedy and harms living things.
"Interval energy" (*jiànqì*) refers to that which appears not every generation; such are those like Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou.
It is also said to refer to individuals who transcend the ordinary, being beyond the concerns of the mundane world.
To possess wealth is called "rich"; to possess emolument is called "noble.
*Cǐ* (泚) is pronounced with the *qiān* and *lǐ* finals.
It means clear water. A mirror reflects images; beauty and ugliness cannot escape it. Just as a stream or pond reflects the sky above, a precious mirror reveals even a single hair.
It is impossible to evade; it requires no artificial effort.
○ Loyalty (*zhong*) means to exhaust one’s own sincerity; benevolence (*shu*) means to allow others their due.
These are words that may seem vulgar and commonplace, yet they represent the integrity I maintain—firm, upright, and unyielding.
"Ji-liang" (伎倆) means skillful artistry and many talents; it is a colloquial term meaning "not particularly important.
Regarding the attendant Fang: Chan Master Chaozong Huifang of Heshan in Jizhou was a successor of Chan Master Huanglong Nan.
He belonged to the twelfth generation under Mount Heng.
The countenance of compassionate sorrow and the appearance of sympathetic empathy—caressing those above brings them peace;
guiding those below ensures their compliance. This is the principle of humbling one's dignity to accord with the lowly.

"Centrality and harmony mean that principles are without partiality and affairs are without urgency or laxity. Furthermore, when joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure have not yet been manifested, it is called 'centrality' (zhong);
when they are manifested and all accord with the proper measure, it is called 'harmony' (he)."
"Vengeful" (*chóu*) refers to the intent to repay an offense with resentment; it denotes a mind that admits no leniency.
"Gǒu" (pronounced *hòu*) means anger; it also implies pursuit.
"Quán-háo" refers to those who hold office and possess power—these are the "quán"—and those whose wealth and strength are both superior—these are the "háo."
*Wang* means "non-existent. It is the stirring of a stimulus that awakens one's loyalty.
**Chanyuan Tong:** Chan Master Fashu Yuancong of Fayun Monastery in Bianliang.
He was the son of the Xin family of Longcheng in Qinzhou and succeeded Chan Master Tianyi Huai as his dharma heir. He belonged to the eleventh generation of the Qingyuan lineage.

Regarding "fèn" (忿): the lower character is written as "chì" (懥) in the original text. The upper part signifies the intensity of anger; the lower part signifies the stagnation of anger. Regarding "fèn" (憤):
it refers to the mind desiring to be unblocked but being unable to achieve it yet.
*Fei*: To be reluctant to speak; it refers to the desire to speak from the mouth but being unable to do so.
*Hxiang-dang*: One hundred and twenty thousand households constitute a *xiang*; five hundred households constitute a *dang*. *Shang-jiā*:
(The second character) has the low tone *gǔ*. This refers to itinerant merchants (*shāng*) and shopkeepers (*jiā*).
To slaughter is called *tu*; to sell wine is called *gu*.
